q: Walk through a production RAG architecture.
a: Gateway (SSO, rate limits) → async orchestrator (history, cache, rewrite) → retrieval service (permission-filtered hybrid search + rerank) → LLM gateway (routing, fallback, cost) → model, streamed back via SSE; guardrails and tracing. Separate ingestion workers fed by a queue; Postgres, Redis, vector index and S3 as stores.

q: Where does most of a RAG request's latency go?
a: LLM generation (output tokens ÷ tokens/s), then any extra LLM calls (rewrite, checks), then reranking. Stream the answer, keep prompts lean, use small models for auxiliary calls, run steps in parallel.

q: How do you enforce document permissions in RAG?
a: Store access groups as chunk metadata and filter inside the retrieval query using the user's SSO identity. Never rely on the LLM to hide content; include scope in cache keys.
SSE: one-way server-to-client stream over HTTP, simplest for streaming answers. WebSockets: two-way, for interactive agents (interrupt, approve). Both need async servers and longer proxy timeouts.

q: Which parts of a RAG system should be separate services?
a: Ingestion workers (batch, bursty) and any self-hosted GPU models (embeddings, reranker, LLM). API and orchestration can stay a modular monolith.
